uniequip_002_toledo:
Kill the sea.
Every Iberian who longs to join the Inquisition carries this resolve to some degree, and so do I. But I can only repeat it silently to myself, because in my hands there is no rapier, only a shovel for planting sugarcane. In every town along the Iberian coast there must be people who think as I do; some of them joined the Punitive Army, and some of them died. This town is remote, and the Inquisitors come on patrol to recruit only once every two years. This year that time has come again, but clearly they are late, or they will never come again. I have seen the horrors of the Sea Terrors, and I know what joining the Punitive Army means, but I need a real weapon, like an Inquisition rapier. I pray that strength will free me from my fear of the sea, and revive this forgotten town.
A stranger came to town. Not an Inquisitor, but a small Liberi lodging here. She was dressed very grandly and had a very long name, apparently the descendant of some noble. Every day she gave speeches in the square, and many people went to listen; the laughter and gasps carried all the way to the shore. I didn't care where she came from. What I saw was the sword at her waist: a proper weapon, one that could stand against Sea Terrors and the tides, that could truly let a person accomplish something. A pity it was not in my hands.
The people following that noble grew in number, and they gestured and measured all over town. Getting the mayor's approval took some effort on her part. I didn't understand why she didn't simply draw her sword. Was it only an ornament? The chance to find out came soon enough. The noble walked into my field and tasted the water used for irrigation and the withered sugarcane. If she wanted to buy this land, I would be more than glad; so long as I could join the Inquisition afterward, I would never return to this barren town. Hearing me out, she drew her sword, and now she truly looked like a conqueror. Then she drove that beautiful weapon into the ground, pulled it out again, rubbed the grains of soil on its tip between her fingers, and proposed a deal.
"You want to put up your sword as collateral, in exchange for my shovel?"
"That's right, just for a little while."
The noble drove the shovel into the ground and twisted it. As expected, she was not suited to farm work; it looked like a real struggle. Still, the color of the sandy soil gradually darkened, and water seeped up from below, pooling in the hole like a little sea.
"There's fresh water underground not far from your field. Hook it up to Rhodes Island's irrigation system, and it will keep your bellies full for the coming year. This I promise you, as the descendant of the Iberian Royal Navy, the great Lady de Toledo."
"A descendant of the navy... with a shovel? Planting sugarcane?"
"Does that bother you? I'm fulfilling my 'Noblesse Oblige'! Besides, I tried digging with my sword, and it was far too inefficient. What about you, coming here with a shovel every day to look at the sea? It never occurred to you to dig into the ground?"
I looked at the field beneath my feet and the noble's sword stuck in the earth, and for a moment I forgot both the Inquisition and the roaring sea. The noble who called herself de Toledo said she would stay in town, and invited me to join the team building the irrigation system. Perhaps once the sugarcane ripens, I can ask her to lend me that sword to peel it.
